title: X Feed Digest
summary: Agent tooling kept maturing from hacker workflows into governed products: OpenAI shipped Codex hooks and workspace-scoped tokens, while Google Cloud rolled out a full Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

The coding-agent conversation was unusually operational today. The strongest posts were about cost, uptime, automation hooks, and shared state — plus fresh complaints that GPT-5.5 quality may have slipped.
Creative AI is still moving fast: Krea unveiled its own image foundation model, and the feed kept treating aesthetic control as a serious product differentiator rather than a toy feature.

On the market side, the dominant throughline was still compute plus electricity scarcity. Bullish takes on AI-linked power demand were everywhere, with follow-on discussion about grid constraints and the real cost of bad energy bets.

Security and credibility mattered too: a new node-ipc compromise was the clearest immediate engineering risk, and SpacetimeDB’s public benchmark correction was a good reminder not to treat vendor numbers as gospel.

items.title: @OpenAIDevs: Codex Hooks + Scoped Tokens
items.body: OpenAI added hooks that let teams run validators, secret scans, logging, and repo-specific automation inside the Codex loop, plus workspace-scoped access tokens for CI and internal tooling. The big shift is that Codex is getting easier to govern and embed into real production workflows.

items.title: @googlecloud: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
items.body: Google Cloud launched an enterprise platform for building, scaling, governing, and optimizing Gemini-based agents. It is a meaningful signal that the agent stack is consolidating into official platform products instead of scattered custom glue.

items.title: @krea_ai: Krea 2 Foundation Model
items.body: Krea introduced Krea 2 as its first image foundation model built in-house, positioning aesthetic range and stylistic control as the headline features. The interesting part is not just another model launch, but the emphasis on taste and controllability as product moat.

items.title: @sickdotdev: Codex vs Claude Code After Two Weeks
items.body: A useful practitioner report said GPT-5.5 high-effort in Codex was materially cheaper, more stable, and often better at code generation than the author’s recent Claude Code setup, though Claude still had the stronger plugin ecosystem. It was one of the better real-world workflow comparisons in the batch because it focused on cost and uptime, not vibes.

items.title: @mweinbach: GPT-5.5 Quality Drift Watch
items.body: Max Weinbach flagged a same-day drop in GPT-5.5 pass rates and said the model felt worse in practice, with a separate post citing a 6% decline from Margin Labs. It is only a feed-level signal for now, but it stood out because it matches the kind of silent regression developers actually care about.

items.title: @APompliano: Compute + Power Shortage Bull Case
items.body: Pompliano’s core thesis was that the stock bull run still has room because the market is underestimating how severe the compute and power shortage is. Even allowing for the usual Pompliano volume, the post captured the feed’s clearest macro consensus: AI demand is increasingly an electricity story.

items.title: @Protectaxpayers: PJM Electricity Rates Are Climbing
items.body: A widely shared energy-policy post argued that electricity prices in PJM states are rising faster than in much of the country and tied that to weak competition. The actionable read is that grid bottlenecks and power-market design are staying front and center as second-order AI trades.

items.title: @porterstansb: Berkshire Energy as a Cautionary Tale
items.body: Porter Stansberry made the case that Berkshire Hathaway Energy absorbed decades of capital on a Peak Oil worldview that did not play out, leaving the business exposed to write-downs, wildfire liabilities, and poor economics on parts of its renewable build-out. Whether or not you buy the full framing, it was one of the sharper deep-commentary posts on capital allocation risk in the batch.

items.title: @pstAsiatech: The Washington “AI Race” Narrative
items.body: Paul Triolo amplified a piece arguing that Silicon Valley’s framing of an all-out U.S.-China AI race may rest on real misunderstandings of China’s actual priorities. The market implication is that a lot of policy, subsidy, and regulatory behavior may be getting built on a story that is less solid than it looks.

items.title: @feross: node-ipc Compromised Again
items.body: Feross flagged three malicious node-ipc releases and said the payload can steal cloud credentials, SSH keys, env vars, and other secrets via DNS exfiltration after an expired-domain account takeover. If your stack touched those versions, the practical advice was blunt: audit lockfiles and rotate secrets immediately.

items.title: @spacetime_db: Benchmark Retraction
items.body: SpacetimeDB said a serious internal error made its March benchmark numbers misleading and publicly walked them back. It was a valuable credibility post because it highlighted how easy it is for benchmark claims to outrun reality, even from teams willing to publish methodology.

items.title: @SahilExec: The Rate Limiter Smell Test
items.body: A simple interview-style prompt exposed two classic mistakes at once: returning HTTP 200 for a rate-limit error and treating request counts as naive app logic rather than a durable shared control. It was a compact reminder that correctness under load usually belongs in infrastructure, not just in if-statements.

items.title: @LukeGrahamWhite: Don’t Time Supercycles by Numerology
items.body: Luke Graham White argued that secular bull and bear regimes are driven by institutions, capital migration, and political response, not neat calendar rhythms. It was a good corrective to the feed’s lazier “AI boom means X by 2034” style of market storytelling.
